title: WTH does every dashboard subscribe to every entity with no way to filter updates?
text: Problem Home Assistant’s frontend subscribes to every single entity in the home and streams every state change to all dashboards regardless of what entities are actually being used or shown on the dashboard. In most cases, this is probably not noticeable, but it can become a problem for large setups with thousands of entities, especially if you have noisy entities like some mmwave presence sensors that publish updates several times a second. This is especially noticeable for low-powered always on kiosks or wall tablets. Real life example I run several Sonoff NSPanel Pros as minimalist room controllers, plus an Android wall tablet for our main home dashboard. Even though each NSPanel dashboard only had a handful of cards, they were sluggish, unresponsive, and frequently disconnected. Eventually, I realised that this was because there were too many updates being sent to the panels for them to keep up. This manifested in the logs as: Logger: homeassistant.components.websocket_api.http.connection Client unable to keep up with pending messages. Stayed over 1024 for 10 seconds. The system's load is too high or an integration is misbehaving; Complex workarounds I am not alone in this problem. Doing some digging, I found this thread with users facing the same issue. That thread led me to a rather unconventional workaround: to create a second instance of HA using Remote Home-Assistant , replicating only the entities I needed for the dashboard, and pointing my NSPanel devices to the remote instance, effectively making a proxy that only forwards the relevant entity updates. Since then, there have been other community projects that specifically try to solve this problem: HA-Websocket-Stripper - A dedicated reverse-proxy add-on built specifically to rewrite unfiltered subscribe_entities and get_states calls per dashboard so wall tablets and kiosks load quickly. HA-Strimmer - A fork that adds more filtering for entity/device/area registries, custom card JS bundles, and service lists per dashboard. Kiosk Satellite - Dedicated kiosk browser with built in support for client side filtering of dashboard updates, with automatic detection of relevant entities per dashboard. I myself have since switched to Kiosk Satellite and the automatic entity detection works great for my dashboards! The ask HA’s backend WebSocket API ( subscribe_entities ) already supports passing a list of entity_id s for filtering, and even include/exclude filtering . There should be some native way to filter the subscribed entities to avoid receiving updates from unrelated entities in the UI. This could be: Automatic detection and filtering of state change updates for each dashboard based on what cards and entities are displayed (like Kiosk Satellite). Per dashboard / per integration / per entity setting to manually include/exclude state updates from being sent to frontend dashboards (like Remote Home-assistant, HA-Websocket-stripper or HA-Strimmer). This optimisation would save bandwidth, compute and battery life, making setting up dedicated wall panels with low powered Android devices much easier and more responsive. 2 posts - 2 participants Read full topic
triage_reason: Home Assistant frontend streams all state changes without filtering.

title: WTH: Why is managing Zigbee2MQTT entities in Home Assistant so unnecessarily painful?
text: Every time I add a new Zigbee device through Zigbee2MQTT, I have to go through the same frustrating process. There are three issues that really should be addressed. 1. Why are Link Quality and Last Seen entities disabled by default? Every time I add a device, I have to manually enable the Link Quality and Last Seen entities. Why are these disabled in the first place? I appreciate that some devices expose a large number of entities, many of which may never be used. However, in my opinion, Link Quality and Last Seen are pretty fundamental diagnostic entities for anything beyond a basic Zigbee setup. Why can’t we configure which entities should be enabled or disabled by default? Ideally, there should be a system-wide configuration option that allows users to define their preferred defaults, rather than having to repeat the same process for every new device. 2. Why does enabling a single entity cause the entire MQTT integration to reload? This is probably the most frustrating issue. When I enable a previously disabled entity, Home Assistant appears to reload every device in the MQTT integration. On my system, which has a large number of devices, it takes approximately 4–5 minutes for everything to return to normal. All this disruption simply because I’ve enabled one entity! I can’t understand why enabling an entity on one device should affect every other device in the integration. Surely it should be possible to enable an entity without disrupting the entire MQTT integration? 3. Why doesn’t renaming a device update its disabled entities? When a new device is added through Zigbee2MQTT, it initially appears with an IEEE address as its name, something like: 0xc09b9efffef6430e Naturally, I want to rename it to something meaningful, such as: shed_temperature_humidity_sensor I’ve found that I need to do this in Zigbee2MQTT because Home Assistant’s Recreate Entity IDs functionality doesn’t always work correctly in this situation. But here’s the next problem: disabled entities don’t get renamed! So I end up with entities such as: sensor.0xc09b9efffef6430e_linkquality instead of: sensor.shed_temperature_humidity_sensor_linkquality I then have to manually restore the entity IDs to get everything consistent. Why aren’t disabled entities included when entity IDs are recreated or renamed? What I’d like to see A configurable default for which entities are automatically enabled when new devices are discovered. Enabling or disabling an entity should not cause unrelated MQTT devices to become temporarily unavailable. Renaming devices or recreating entity IDs should include disabled entities, not just enabled ones. I have a fairly large Home Assistant installation, and these issues become increasingly frustrating as the number of devices grows. None of these should require so much manual intervention. Surely there must be a better way! 12 posts - 6 participants Read full topic
triage_reason: Managing Zigbee2MQTT entities forces repetitive manual enabling steps.

title: How are you deciding what to reorder since Stocky shut down?
text: Curious how other shops are handling this now that Stocky’s reorder suggestions are gone. The simplest method I’ve found: • Days left = stock ÷ average daily sales • Reorder when days left ≤ supplier delivery time + about a week • Order enough to cover delivery time + the next month, minus what’s already on order The part most people get wrong is using the delivery time the supplier quotes instead of how long they actually take. What’s working for you: spreadsheet, an app, or just going by feel? 6 posts - 4 participants Read full topic
triage_reason: Merchants lack reorder suggestions after Shopify shut down Stocky.

title: HTML Max Charachters in Blogs
text: We have migrated to Shopify and are super happy after going live last week. The one area where I have a challenge, however, is that we have a few dozen pages that I need to dump some frankenstein HTML into to keep the styling as it was in our previous site. However, I found that for many of the pages, I couldn’t save the draft and publish it to the site. It turned out it wasn’t able to handle all that HTML. It seemed like the buffer wasn’t big enough to write it all in at save. However, what I found was that if I did it in chunks at a time (put in a quarter of it, save it, put in another quarter of it, save it, put in another quarter of it, save it), it worked. But this slows the process down considerably. I’m wondering if there is any way around this or if people know what the max character count is for saving. Any advice much appreciated. Note: I was using Bloggle to enter the HTML, but even if I did it right through the Shopify blog, the same issue was there. 6 posts - 6 participants Read full topic
triage_reason: Shopify's blog editor fails to save large or complex HTML snippets.

title: How do you track which staff members viewed or exported customer data?
text: Hi everyone, We’re looking at privacy compliance (GDPR/CCPA-type requirements) and I’m trying to understand what other merchants do about access records for customer data in the admin. As far as I can tell, the store activity log only shows changes, can’t be exported, and doesn’t record who viewed a customer or exported the customer list. A few questions: Do you keep any record of which staff opened customer/order pages or exported customer data? How? Has an auditor, customer request, or security incident ever required you to show who accessed what? If you use an app for this, what’s missing from it?
